                      UNITED STATES DISTRICT COURT                           
                     WESTERN DISTRICT OF WASHINGTON                          
9                              AT TACOMA                                     
10                                                                            
11    UNITED STATES OF AMERICA,          CASE NO. 3:20-cv-05867-DGE           
12                   Plaintiff,          ORDER ON MOTION FOR RECUSAL          
          v.                                                                 
13                                                                            
     JOAN V. BAYLEY, et al.,                                                 
14                                                                            
                    Defendants.                                              
15                                                                            

16       This is a pro se civil rights action against numerous defendants. This matter is before the 
17  Court on Defendant Philip N. Bayley’s amended motion to recuse Judge David Estudillo (Dkt. 
18  No. 289) and Judge Estudillo’s order denying and referring the motion to recuse (Dkt. No. 292). 
19  Having reviewed Mr. Bayley’s motion, Judge Estudillo’s order denying the recusal request, Mr. 
20  Bayley’s reply to Judge Estudillo’s order (Dkt. No. 293), Mr. Bayley’s Notice of Objections 
21  (Dkt. No. 295), and the relevant record, the Court AFFIRMS Judge Estudillo’s order denying the 
22  motion to recuse.                                                         
23                           I.   BACKGROUND                                  
24       On February 15, 2024, Mr. Bayley filed a motion to recuse Judge David Estudillo and 
1  “the entire Western District of Washington active-status Judges.” Dkt. No. 289 at 1. On February 
2  20, 2024, Judge Estudillo declined to voluntarily recuse and referred the motion to this Court for 
3  decision. See Dkt. No. 292 at 5.                                          
4                         II.  LEGAL STANDARD                                

5       Local Civil Rule (“LCR”) (3)(f) requires a challenged judge to review motions filed 
6  pursuant to 28 U.S.C. § 144 or 28 U.S.C. § 455 and to determine whether to recuse voluntarily. 
7  LCR 3(f). If the challenged judge declines to recuse voluntarily, the judge must direct the court 
8  clerk to refer the motion to the chief judge for their review. Id. If the motion is directed at the 
9  chief judge, or if the chief judge (or their designee) is unavailable, the clerk must refer the 
10  motion to the active judge with the highest seniority. Id.                
11       28 U.S.C. § 455(a) provides that judges of the United States “shall disqualify [themselves 
12  in any proceeding in which [their] impartiality might reasonably be questioned.” The statute 
13  further provides that judges must recuse “[w]here [they have] a personal bias or prejudice 
14  concerning a party, or personal knowledge of disputed evidentiary facts concerning the 

15  proceeding.” 28 U.S.C. § 455(b)(1). Similarly, 28 U.S.C. § 144 requires recusal when “a party to 
16  any proceeding in a district court makes and files a timely and sufficient affidavit that the judge 
17  before whom the matter is pending has a personal bias or prejudice either against [them] or in 
18  favor of any adverse party.” The standard for recusal under both statutes is the same: “Whether a 
19  reasonable person with knowledge of all the facts would conclude that the judge’s impartiality 
20  might reasonably be questioned.” United States v. McTiernan, 695 F.3d 882, 891 (9th Cir. 2012) 
21  (internal citation omitted). “The alleged prejudice must result from an extrajudicial source; a 
22  judge’s prior adverse ruling is not sufficient cause for recusal.” United States v. Studley, 783 
23  F.2d 934, 939 (9th Cir. 1986) (internal citation omitted); see also Liteky v. United States, 510 

24                                                                            
1  U.S. 540, 555 (1994) (“[J]udicial rulings alone almost never constitute a valid basis for a bias or 
2  partiality recusal motion.”) (internal citation omitted).                 
3                            III.  DISCUSSION                                
4       As an initial matter, this motion is before this Court because Chief Judge David Estudillo 

5  referred the motion pursuant to Local Civil Rule 3(f). Dkt. No. 292 at 5. 
6       In seeking Judge Estudillo’s recusal, Mr. Bayley references some comments he heard 
7  Judge Estudillo make at a public presentation entitled “Not Lost in Translation: Innovations in 
8  Language Access” that was held on February 8, 2024. See generally Dkt. Nos. 289, 290. Mr. 
9  Bayley states that he heard Judge Estudillo discuss the importance of “effective communication, 
10  parties feeling heard and understood, unwavering respect owed to all parties and equal access to 
11  justice.” Dkt. No. 289 at 2. Yet, Mr. Bayley feels that “the Chief Judge either ignores 
12  Defendants’ arguments or brushes them off without effectively communicating in a manner that 
13  makes the Defendant feel heard, understood, or respected and that their arguments have been 
14  fully considered by the Court.” Id. at 3–4. In particular, Mr. Bayley asserts that Judge Estudillo 

15  did not adequately consider Defendants’ arguments and authorities. Id. at 3; see also Dkt. No 293 
16  at 1–2; Dkt. No. 295 at 2. While it is regrettable that Mr. Bayley does not feel adequately heard 
17  or understood, his challenge essentially boils down to a disagreement with Judge Estudillo’s 
18  rationale in his rulings and how he applied the law to the facts in this case. But “a judge’s prior 
19  adverse ruling is not sufficient cause for recusal.” Studley, 783 F.2d at 939. The basis for recusal 
20  generally requires something other than judicial rulings or “opinions formed by the judge on the 
21  basis of facts introduced or events occurring in the course of the current proceedings.” Liteky, 
22  510 U.S. at 554-56; accord United States v. Holland, 519 F.3d 909, 913–14 (9th Cir. 2008). 
23  “Almost invariably,” rather than a basis for recusal, judicial rulings are a basis for appeal. Id. at 

24  555.                                                                      
1       To the extent Mr. Bayley asserts that comments Judge Estudillo made at the public 
2  presentation are an extrajudicial source that revealed a “lack of impartiality between the parties 
3  in this case” (Dkt. No. 289 at 1), it is unclear how any of the comments cited by Mr. Bayley in 
4  his declaration (Dkt. No. 290)1 would call into question Judge Estudillo’s impartiality in this 

5  case, especially since no interpreters appear to be involved in this case at all. Cf. McTiernan, 695 
6  F.3d at 891 (stating the standard for determining whether recusal is warranted). Mr. Bayley also 
7  asserts that Judge Estudillo “has weaponized his Western Washington District Court and all 
8  active status subordinate judges to enact his prejudices.” Dkt. No. 289 at 5; see also Dkt. No. 295 
9  at 1 (contending that “the entire United States District Court Western District of Washington is 
10  compromised, weaponized, and polluted with his prejudices and instructions to his subservient 
11  judges to deploy vindictive retaliations”). The only potential example he gives is that Judge 
12  Estudillo has “brag[ged] about weaponizing Judge Tana Kim (whom his [sic] own comments 
13  should disqualify her from weighing in on his denial of my motion to recuse him).” Dkt. No. 
14  293 at 3 (emphasis in original); Dkt. No. 295 at 4 (same). First, Mr. Bayley did not specify the 

15  comments “Tana Kim” made that should disqualify her from ruling on the present motion. 
16  Second, the undersigned believes Mr. Bayley has referenced her in his statement about “Tana 
17  Kim.” However, it appears that Mr. Bayley has confused the undersigned judge (Tana Lin) with 
18  an interpreter who was a panelist at the public presentation (Eunyoung Kim). See Dkt. No. 292 at 
19  3–4. The undersigned did not attend, participate in, or make any comments at the public 
20  presentation at issue.                                                    
21                                                                            
22                                                                            

   1 No audio or video of the presentation is available, so the Court will accept the accuracy of Mr. Bayley’s 
23                                                                            
   representations regarding comments made by Judge Estudillo for purposes of this motion to recuse. However, the 
   fact that only small excerpts are included make it difficult to determine if Mr. Bayley’s interpretation of the 
24  comments are either mistaken or perhaps taken out of context.             
1                           IV.  CONCLUSION                                  
2       Having considered Mr. Bayley’s arguments in support of recusal and finding them 
3  without merit, this Court AFFIRMS Judge Estudillo’s order denying Mr. Bayley’s motion to 
4  recuse.                                                                   

5       Dated this 27th day of February 2024.                                
6                                                                            
                                      A                                      
7                                                                            
                                      Tana Lin                               
                                      United States District Judge
